resources.string: This WiFi level is rated on a 1 through 5 scale illustrating the strength of your device to the router. Higher values mean better connectivity (e.g., 5 is best and 1 is weakest). The scale is based off of the RSSI level reading from your connected device.

A Wi-Fi standard refers to a specific version or generation of wireless networking technology, defined by the IEEE 802.11 family of protocols. Each standard introduces improvements in speed, range, reliability, frequency bands, and efficiency.
Shows the supported Wi-Fi capabilities such as WPA/WPA2, PSK, etc.

Channel width in Wi-Fi refers to the amount of frequency spectrum (measured in MHz) used to transmit data.\n\n Higher width means more speed, but also more interference and less compatibility. Lower width is more stable, especially in crowded environments or with older devices.
This is the primary frequency (in MHz) used by your Wi-Fi connection. It helps identify which channel your device is using to send and receive data.
This is the secondary frequency used in wide-channel configurations like 40, 80, or 160 MHz. It helps Wi-Fi devices achieve faster speeds by bonding multiple channels together.

Passpoint is a Wi-Fi standard that allows devices to automatically and securely connect to participating public Wi-Fi networks.\n\n It provides seamless, encrypted, and trusted connections—similar to cellular roaming.
802.11mc is a Wi-Fi standard also known as Wi-Fi Round Trip Time (RTT). It allows devices to measure the distance to nearby Wi-Fi access points using precise timing.
This is the rate at which data is downloaded from the network to your device. A higher downstream speed means faster loading times for videos, files, and web pages.
This is the rate at which data is uploaded from your device to the network. Faster upstream speeds help improve file uploads, video calls, and live streaming.
The gateway is the IP address of the router your device uses to connect to the internet or other networks. It acts as the entry and exit point for network traffic outside your local network.

A netmask (short for network mask) is a number that defines which part of an IP address is the network portion and which part is the host portion.\n\n Think of an IP address like a street address, and the netmask tells you how many houses are on the same street.
This is the main server your device contacts to translate website names into IP addresses. It helps your device find websites and services on the internet quickly.
This is the backup DNS server your device uses if the primary DNS server is unavailable, ensuring continued access to domain name resolution.
The time period your device is allowed to use its current IP address assigned by the network’s DHCP server before it needs to renew or request a new one.
The type of network connection your device is currently using, such as Wi-Fi, Cellular, or Ethernet.
Indicates if your device currently has access to the internet through the connected network.
Indicates whether the device’s network connection has been confirmed to provide internet access by successfully reaching external servers.
Shows if the current network connection has data limits or usage charges, which may restrict background data to save on costs.

The interference value is an estimated representation of how many nearby Wi-Fi networks are operating on frequencies close to your current Wi-Fi connection, which could cause signal interference and affect performance.

The SSID is the name of a Wi-Fi network. It is an acronym for Service Set Identifier.\n\n When you look at a list of Wi-Fi networks on your phone or computer, each name that you see (such as My_Wifi or CoffeeShopABC) is an SSID.

RSSI stands for Received Signal Strength Indicator. It tells how you strong the Wi-Fi signal is between your device and a router or access point.\n\n The closer to 0 the stronger the signal strength, the farther away from 0 the weaker the signal strength.
The WiFi frequency in megahertz (MHz), typically 2400 MHz (2.4 GHz) or 5000 MHz (5 GHz), indicating the radio band used for wireless communication.
This is a common and simplified version of the Wi-Fi frequency your device is using.
The BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier) is the unique MAC address of a Wi-Fi access point (router).\n\n It helps your device know exactly which access point or router it is communicating with..
This is the IPv4 address assigned to your device while on the Wi-Fi network.
The link speed is the rate at which data CAN be transferred between your device and the Wi-Fi router or access point. It is like the speed limit of your connection.
The max link speed is the highest possible data transfer rate between your device and the Wi-Fi router or access point. It is the maximum speed your device COULD achieve.
